## Where the fix belongs, and the precedent search

The feature map puts top-level variable declarations at `Decls.scala` for the checker and `CodeGen.forVarDecl` for the code generator (`explorations/coordinator/map/spec-to-implementation.md:200`). The checker's defect is in the one case that rebuilds the right side; the two other `SVarDecl` cases and the three `SLocalVarDecl` cases of the file keep the checked right side or build it typed, so there is one site, not a family (`Decls.scala:248-326`, `:337-425`). The code generator's precedents are two: the local form (`CodeGen.java:4436`), which evaluates a tuple-valued right side once and picks its pieces with `INVOKEINTERFACE` on the tuple's typed getters, and walk's desugaring, whose comment states the team's design: "Introduce a temporary, then initialize elements piece-by-piece" (`DesugarerVisitor.java:858-859`). The edit follows both: one temporary, pieces by the typed getters.

## What the specification settles

`Specification/basic/variables.tex:99-120`: every form of a top-level declaration can be used with tuple notation, with the types beside the names, as one tuple type, or left out; "especially helpful when a function application returns a tuple of values". `:63` and `:74`: a variable's value "is computed to be the value of the initializer expression", so one evaluation. `:122`: an initializer can refer to variables declared later. P-173 gives a numeral element its default at an untyped name. Nothing there says when a top-level initializer runs; `Specification/basic/components/initialization.tex:15` asks only that every variable is initialized before its use.

## The binding as compiled

- When: the right side is evaluated when the first of its names is first read, in the static initializer of the hidden class, which the JVM runs once. A single top-level variable is evaluated the same way today: `x = one()` with a printing `one` prints 'run starts' before 'one runs'.
- How many times: once. `TopLevelTupleBindingCompiled` asserts `calls = 1` after three reads of the two names at four threads.
- What each name is: a top-level variable of its own class `<Component>$<name>`, immutable or a `MutableFValue` cell, typed by its declared type or its element's type; importing components read it as any exported variable.

The same driver with `full`, which goes on into the code generator:

    @@CG OK	VarDecl [nEmbd:ZZ32, blockSize:ZZ32, nHead:ZZ32, headDim:ZZ32, vocabSize:ZZ32, bosId:ZZ32]	…/MicroGptFlat.fss:17:1-78
    @@CG OK	VarDecl [epsilon:RR64, lr0:RR64, beta1:RR64, beta2:RR64, epsilon_A:RR64, nSteps:ZZ32]	…/MicroGptFlat.fss:18:1-97

Before, the driver met 'tupled lhs not handled' at each of the three (`model-closure-check.md:58`). No line of the model or of its helper files is changed.

## The stages and the timing

Both stages ran once, on `47aad62914`, the final tree: no code changed after their start.

**The count stage.** Against climb batch 30's gate table:

    $ diff explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-30/gate/checker-count.txt <the table of 47aad62914>
    (nothing)
    #total	0
    #locations	0
    #crash	none

**The distance stage.**

    $ explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/compare.sh explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-30/gate/distance.txt <the table of 47aad62914>
    DISTANCE SAME   0
    #seconds	127	FortressLibrary 79
    #shadow	every shadow edit matched the tracked sources

`errors.tsv` of the run and `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv` hold a header and no site, so no site moved. The stage took 129 s of wall time, load at start 3.77.

**P-148's runs** (the skill's `compiler.md`, "The checker's time"), one session, the same command, the other agent's work beside both:

| run | tree | seconds (real) |
|---|---|---|
| base | the base build, `/home/user/fortress-base33` | 92.6 |
| change | `47aad62914` | 80.5 (load at start 2.94) |

The two tables are equal (`diff` prints nothing), and the two `run.txt` files are equal after each tree's path is replaced by one word (`diff` prints nothing; 33 lines each). The second pass changed no code, so there is no `pass` run and no second `ant testQuick`: the interpreter's library has no top-level tuple binding (`grep -n '^(.*) *=' Library/*.fss ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/*.fss` finds none outside comments), so the count stage never runs the changed case, and a JFR profile of the stage (4,809 samples, an instrumented copy of the script under `tmp/`) shows no frame of it. Its top frames are the generated walker's: `Walker.walkCases7$` 361, `walkCases5` 211, `walkCases0` 178, `walkCases2` 173, `ASTGenHelper$.scalaify` 163. The added work is one tuple type for each top-level tuple binding of a tuple expression.

**The ladder subset** of my change: the three files of the baseline whose recorded first error is 'tupled lhs not handled' (`explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/ladder.tsv`: `tests/TupleBinding.fss`, `tests/TupleBinding2.fss`, `tests/Variable.VarWTypes.fss`, each at `codegen`). The gate's 85 do not hold them, so the comparison is with the baseline. After the edit, by `run-subset.sh` and `classify.py` copied under `tmp/rung-tuple-binding/ladder/`:

    tests	TupleBinding.fss		pass
    tests	TupleBinding2.fss		pass
    tests	Variable.VarWTypes.fss		pass

Three files UP, from `codegen` to `pass`. The microGPT components stop at disambiguation under the prelude ('Array is undefined.'), which this change does not reach.

## Sentences of the specification made false

None. `grep -n -i 'tuple binding\|tuple notation\|top-level tuple\|tupled' -r Specification --include=*.tex` outside `Specification-1.0-frozen` finds `basic/variables.tex:99`, `:137` and `basic/expressions/bindings.tex:44`, each the language's rule and none a note on what either path does; `appendices/changes.tex` has no entry on top-level variables.

## Points to report

1. **Where the names' types were lost, and the repair.** `Decls.scala:272-277`, above.
2. **The binding as compiled.** Above: once, at the first read of any name; each name a top-level variable.
3. **Row 988's reproducer and row 474's cases, a numeral element's type, a var binding, a typed one, a call.** The table above and `TopLevelTupleBindingCompiled`.
4. **The model's lines 17 to 19 under the distance stage's driver.** Above: no checker error before or after; the code generator's three throws are three `@@CG OK`; the file's sites go from 8 to 9 (`:41` gone, `:77` twice new).
5. **The count and distance tables, their commit, their seconds, P-148's runs.** Above.
6. **Each sentence of the specification made false.** None.
7. **A file edited beyond those named.** None outside the two named files. Inside `CodeGen.java`, beside `forVarDeclPrePass`, the edit touches `generateVarDeclInnerClass` (an overload added, `:6436-6462`) and `addTopLevelVarBinding` (each name registered, `:6572-6583`), both called only for top-level variables, and adds `forTupleVarDeclPrePass`, `tupleVarDeclHolderClass` and `isWildcard`.
8. **A model line.** None changed. One model line newly reported by the checker against the one library, `MicroGptFlat.fss:77`, above.
9. **A change of how a single top-level binding or a local tuple binding is typed.** None: the edited case runs only for several names.

## Decisions

1. **The right side goes whole into one hidden variable; each name takes its element from it.** Ways not taken: (a) for a right side that is a tuple expression, each name's class evaluates its own element, as the local form does (`CodeGen.java:4436`): each element would then run at the first read of its own name, at different moments, and a right side that is a call would still need the hidden variable, so two mechanisms; (b) a desugaring before the code generator into `t = e; a = t.1 …`: the language has no expression for a tuple's element, and walk's own desugaring of this kind is where its defect is (NEW-D-1). Evidence: fork D1, "the right side is evaluated once"; walk's comment (`DesugarerVisitor.java:858-859`).
2. **The hidden class is named `tuple$<first name>`.** Ways not taken: walk's `WellKnownNames.tempTupleName`, `*tuple_` and the declaration's position, which holds a file path and cannot be a class name; a counter, which would make the name depend on the order of generation. A top-level name is unique in its component and no identifier holds `$`, so the name cannot collide.
3. **A wildcard binds nothing; a binding of wildcards only emits nothing.** Way not taken: a class `<Component>$_`, which two bindings would write twice ('duplicate entry: Wild$tuple$_.class' was the first form's failure). Such a right side is then never evaluated on the compiled path, as an unread single variable's is not.
4. **The checker's repair types the rebuilt tuple; the case stays.** Way not taken: delete the special case and let the general case check the tuple against the tuple of declared types: the special case is the one that gives each untyped name its element's default beside typed names, as `(e: ZZ64, f) = (5, 6.5)`, and that is not this rung's to redo.
5. **The refusal test's `.test` file has the `XXX` prefix and its program a plain name.** Way not taken: a plain `.test` name, which the harness reads as a compile that must succeed (it was red so on the fixed code). The folder's precedent: `XXXCoverageReturnBad.test` over `CoverageReturnBad.fss`.
6. **The three defects met on the way are recorded, not repaired.** Walk is outside this rung's files, and the export check is another declaration of the checker. Each has an `XXX` test and a row.
7. **The compiled path's moment of evaluation is not recorded as a defect.** A top-level variable is initialized at its first read on the compiled path and at load under walk (row 152). The specification asks that a variable is initialized before its use (`initialization.tex:15`), which both do, and the tuple binding follows the single variable. No decision of the curator covers it; I acted on the reading that it is no defect, and list it for the curator.

## Defects and their homes

| defect | home | where |
|---|---|---|
| the checker loses the names' types (rows 988, 474) | 1, repaired | `compiler_tests/TopLevelTupleBindingCompiled`, `XXXTopLevelTupleBindingType.test` |
| the code generator has no case for several names (row 988's notes) | 1, repaired | `compiler_tests/TopLevelTupleBindingCompiled`, `TopLevelTupleBindingImport` |
| under walk the right side of a top-level tuple binding runs once for each name and once more | 2, the specification settles it (`variables.tex:63`, `:74`) | `tests/XXXTopLevelTupleBindingOnceWalk.fss`, row NEW-D-1 |
| under walk an initializer's call that reads a later mutable variable fails | 2 (`variables.tex:122`) | `tests/XXXInitializerCallReadsLaterMutableWalk.fss`, row NEW-D-2 |
| the export check refuses `:=` without `var` under the api's `var` | 2 (`variables.tex:85`) | `compiler_tests/XXXTopLevelVarByAssignExport.test`, row NEW-D-3 |

The first `XXX` test, `XXXTopLevelTupleBindingOnceWalk`, through `harness-one.sh`: as it is, 'FAIL: a ZZ32: 3 =/= a ZZ32: 1; the right side ran once … OK Saw expected exception', `OK (2 tests)` with the second; with its three expected values set to what walk gives (3, 2, 30) for one run, then restored, 'Missing expected failure', `Tests run: 1,  Failures: 1`.

NEW-D-1 in detail. `DesugarerVisitor.forVarDecl` makes a temporary for the right side and then builds each name's initializer as a field reference `$i` on `init`, the right side's expression, not on the temporary (`DesugarerVisitor.java:865-875`). So for n names the right side runs n + 1 times, and each name holds an element of a run of its own:

    $ bin/fortress WalkOnce2.fss        # (a1, a2) = pairA(); (b1, b2, b3) = tripleB(); each prints when it runs
    A runs
    A runs
    A runs
    B runs
    B runs
    B runs
    B runs

Row 152 says of an earlier model program's `(corpusTokens, corpusLengths) = loadCorpus(corpusPath)` that "the corpus loads once, on import as on run"; by this defect that right side runs three times; I did not run that program, which is only in git history. Today's two model programs bind only tuples of literals this way (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss:17-19`, `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss:26-28`), so they pay only the cost of `10.0^(-5)` seven times.

## Commands worked out

- The count stage under JFR: a copy of `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh` under `tmp/` with `-XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=<file>,settings=profile` put before `-Xmx4g` on its `java` line; then `jfr print --events jdk.ExecutionSample --stack-depth 64 <file>` and a count of the first frame of each sample.

## Questions for the curator

1. Walk's defect NEW-D-1 is one word of `DesugarerVisitor.java:873`: the field reference should be on the temporary. It is outside this rung. Repair it in a rung of walk, or leave it until walk is retired?
2. The moment of a top-level variable's initialization differs between the paths: at load, in declaration order, under walk (row 152); at the first read on the compiled path, also for a single variable. A program whose initializers write mutable state can see it. Is the compiled path's lazy initialization the design, or a gap to record?

=== compiler_tests/TopLevelTupleBindingCompiled.fss
(* A top-level tuple binding declares each name as a variable of its
   element's type, and evaluates its right side once
   (variables.tex, section "Top-Level Variable Declarations"). *)
component TopLevelTupleBindingCompiled
export Executable

(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead) = (16, 8, 4)
(half, quarter) = (0.5, 0.25)
(count: ZZ64, title: String) = (7, "seven")
(lo, hi): (ZZ32, ZZ32) = (3, 5)
(quotient, remainder) = divide(17, 5)
var (ups, downs): (ZZ32, ZZ32) = (1, 2)
(_, kept) = divide(9, 4)
(_, alsoKept) = (0, 5)
var calls: ZZ32 = 0
(first, second) = pairOnce()

divide(a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32): (ZZ32, ZZ32) = (a DIV b, a REM b)

pairOnce(): (ZZ32, ZZ32) = do
    calls += 1
    (calls, 10 calls)
end

run(): () = do
    (* an integer numeral's name is a ZZ32, a float numeral's an RR64 *)
    width: ZZ32 = nEmbd
    share: RR64 = half
    assert(width, 16, "nEmbd")
    assert(nEmbd blockSize + nHead, 132, "integer names in arithmetic")
    assert(share + quarter = 0.75, "float names in arithmetic")
    (* names with declared types *)
    seven: ZZ64 = 7
    assert(count = seven, "count")
    assert(title, "seven", "title")
    assert(hi - lo, 2, "one tuple type for both names")
    (* a right side that is a call *)
    assert(quotient, 3, "quotient")
    assert(remainder, 2, "remainder")
    (* a wildcard binds nothing *)
    assert(kept + alsoKept, 6, "names beside wildcards")
    (* mutable names *)
    ups += 10
    downs := downs - 5
    assert(ups, 11, "ups")
    assert(downs, -3, "downs")
    (* the right side runs once, whichever name is read, and however often *)
    assert(second, 10, "second")
    assert(first, 1, "first")
    assert(first + second, 11, "both again")
    assert(calls, 1, "the right side ran once")
    println("PASS")
end

end

# The compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime

**count stage**
: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library, on the `FortressLibrary` component and the apis that it imports, and prints the errors in a table: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total is the checker count.

**distance stage**
: Stage of the gate that runs the compiled checker over fourteen components of the interpreter's library, `FortressLibrary` among them, runs each of the checker's steps on each component whatever the earlier steps report, and prints the errors in a table. Your brief gives its command when you need it.

The code of this area is in these directories:

- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.

The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.

## What the two paths share

After the phases, each path has its own code for these:

- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
- Number natives: walk's glue classes, in `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`).
- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.

Both paths run the helpers, the public static methods of classes under `nativeHelpers/`.

The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.

## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over

The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.

Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over, and their tests stay. The one exception is the numerals: until then, the prelude's numeral types and its coercions from them follow `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers" (P-37). If a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is wrong, fix the helper's Java, even where the prelude binds it too. Do not edit the prelude's text: its binding then gives the fixed result. If a compiled test pinned the old result, change the test with the helper, as for any fixed defect.

## What the compiled path cannot compile yet

For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:

- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
- an object expression;
- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.

It compiles a local function as a closure, also one that calls itself or another local function of its block. It refuses these forms (ledger row 304):

- a local function with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet';
- two local functions of one name in a block: 'Can't compile overloaded local functions yet';
- a local function with the `atomic` modifier: 'Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet'.

A type assumption `e asif T` has the value of `e`, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if `e` were a `T`, a supertype of `e`'s type (`Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex`). The code generator compiles one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call of a functional method or an overloaded function whose every argument is an assumption, and elsewhere as the value of `e`. It refuses these forms (ledger row 818):

- a call of a functional method or an overloaded function with an assumption at some of its arguments but not all: 'Can't compile a dispatched call whose arguments are not all type assumptions';
- a generic method on an assumed receiver: 'Can't compile a type assumption at the receiver of a generic method yet';
- a call of an overloaded generic function with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet'.

It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. A call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, links, but dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 867). `compiler_tests/XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled.test` records it: copy its form for such a call. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private`, `abstract` and `test`, such as `override` (ledger row 650). A trait or object that extends a generic trait compiles with `Any` as the static argument. With `Bottom`, `Self` or an abbreviated type there, the code generator refuses the declaration. An abbreviated type is a short form, such as `RR64[3]` for an array type. With a tuple that holds `Any` there, the code generator crashes (ledger row 889).

The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.

Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).

## What the code generator does

- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
- It runs a program's own `coerce` from a numeral once for each place where the numeral is written, in the component class's static initializer, except where the place's type names a type parameter (below). The runtime initializes the class of each component that the program's classes name before `run()`, in one task. So a coercion's output comes before the program's first line, and the parallel parts of a coercion's body run one after another there. A coercion that raises stops the program before `run()`. A test of a coercion that raises sets `run_exits_nonzero=true` (`tests-writing.md`).
- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
- The `value` modifier adds the mark interface `ValueObjectMark` to the object's class. The compiled `SEQV` (`nativeHelpers/equality.java`) reads the mark. The modifier does not inline or unbox the fields.
- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet. If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'

## The runtime

- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches. From the switch-over, it also tracks each element of the one library's arrays, by array and index: `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java` calls the transaction's methods `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`. Walk does not run this class, so test an edit of it with `ArrayStoreJUTest`, beside it.

## Natives

`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.

A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. In a compile, at the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). The compile stops in these cases:

- If the string is in that package but names no public static method: 'builtinPrimitive names no static helper: …'.
- If the string names a glue class or anything else outside that package: 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.'
- If the declaration has a varargs parameter: the same message (ledger row 849).
- If the declaration is a local function or a method of an object expression: the same message. The rewrite reaches only a component's declarations and the members of its traits and objects (ledger row 865).

The rewrite runs only in a JVM that has made a Fortress repository of the compiled path, the compiler's store of components, not this git repository. Walk's repository switches it off again. `fortress compile` makes one, and so do `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` and `typecheck` (`Shell.compilerPhases`). `fortress parse` and `fortress api` make none, so they rewrite a body only after a compile in the same JVM (ledger row 882). Alone, they pass a misspelt helper. Test a binding with `compile`. In a suite, the result of `parse` or `api` depends on whether a compile ran earlier in the same JVM.

To test a helper on the compiled path, write a compiled test whose own declarations bind it, as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` does. Until the switch-over, a compiled test cannot reach the interpreter's library's bindings.

The count stage and the distance stage check the interpreter's library with the same rewrite. There, the checker differs from a compile in these ways:

- A string that names a glue class, or a declaration with a varargs parameter, does not stop the check. The body stays a call of `builtinPrimitive`, typed at the declared result type, and no Java signature checks it (ledger row 849).
- The checker reads a helper's Java types as the interpreter's library's types: `String` as `String`, not `JavaString`, and the rest as in a compile.
- A component that imports a DSL grammar is parsed by other code (`GraphRepository.syntaxExpand`), which does not rewrite its bindings. So, as for a glue class, no Java signature checks them.
- The count stage checks only the `FortressLibrary` component's bindings. A binding of another component, as `FortressBuiltin`'s, only the distance stage checks.

The checker, in a compile and in both stages, reads `int` as `NN32` or `Char`, and `long` as `NN64`, only for six transfer helpers with fixed names (`NamingCzar.java:373-384`, `:494-503`). Where a binding gives a parameter, `self` or the result the type `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char`, or a parameter or `self` the type `UnsignedLong` (the one library's object that extends `NN64`), and the helper has `int` or `long` there, the rewrite passes that value through the matching transfer helper. A result declared `UnsignedLong` gets none. `self` gets a transfer helper only in a method of one of these four types itself. The transfer helpers return their argument unchanged. So the checker accepts such a binding whatever helper it names, a signed one included, as `simpleIntArith.intLT` for `NN32`'s `<`. If you move a binding over these types onto a helper, test it on both paths at values where a signed and an unsigned reading differ (2^31 and above for `NN32`, 2^63 and above for `NN64`), as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Compiled.fss` and `tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Walk.fss` do. If the class has more than one method of the helper's name and number of parameters, the rewrite adds no transfer helper. The checker then reports 'Could not check call to function builtinPrimitive_<Class>_<method>', followed by '… is not applicable to an argument of type …'.

The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method. In the count stage and the distance stage, a type maps only if the interpreter's library declares it. So there, a binding stops its component if any method of its helper's class has a type that only the compiler's prelude declares. The distance stage then counts the component as a stopped target. `nativeHelpers/systemOps` is such a class: its `getArgs` answers `StringVector`, so the message is 'FortressBuiltin.StringVector is undefined.' (F-321). Bind a helper of another class.

## Traps of the compiled path

- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit. The prelude's `||` takes the string first only, so `c || s` for a `Character` value `c` is refused (ledger row 965). Put a string first, as `("" || c) || s`.
- A `try`'s `forbid` clause lists exception types: an exception of a listed type that no `catch` clause took is wrapped in a `ForbiddenException`, which the `try` throws. A `try`'s `finally` clause does not run when an exception leaves the `try` block: one that no `catch` clause takes, or that `ForbiddenException` (ledger row 890). So write no compiled program that relies on `finally` after an exception leaves the `try`. A test that needs it is an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`). A `try` whose block can throw, with a `finally` clause and no `catch` or `forbid` clause, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load (ledger row 891).
- To fork is to run as tasks that can run at once. A call's arguments and an operator's operands fork, as the rule says, where two or more of them are calls, written `f(x)`, of functions that the program declares. So write no compiled program that relies on the order in which its arguments are evaluated. Until the switch-over, the calls written in the compiler's prelude do not fork, so a compiled `SUM` runs one body at a time (ledger row 982). A compiled parallel `for` runs its bodies at once: use it in a test of parallelism.
- An `atomic` block or a `try` as a call's argument after the first, as `f(k, atomic do ... end)`, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load, unless the arguments fork (ledger row 322). So does a `try` as an operator's operand after the first (ledger row 526). Bind its value in a statement of its own.
- Numerals and sizes depart from `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways:
  - At a place whose type names a type parameter of its generic declaration, a numeral's coercion runs at each evaluation (ledger row 957). If the body needs the value at one instance only, bind it once, at a top-level variable whose type names no type parameter.
  - Until the switch-over, `RR64` converts only an `RR32` and a numeral, and `RR32` only a numeral. So a `ZZ32` value where an `RR64` is expected is refused (ledger row 442). Write `i.asRR64` for a `ZZ32` value `i`.
  - A numeral with a radix point at a place that fixes no type, which rounds to an infinity at `RR64`, gives `Infinity`, as under walk (ledger row 980). Assert no value for it in a test.
  - A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, raises a `java.lang.Error` that no `catch` sees (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
  - As a `typecase`'s selector, a numeral keeps its own type, as `NaturalNumeral[\1,10,7\]`, so `typecase 7 of ZZ32 => ...` is refused as unreachable (ledger row 963). Bind the selector to a variable first, as `x = 7`, then write `typecase x of ...`.
- A `typecase` tuple pattern with an untyped binder, as `(x, y: ZZ32)`, stops the code generator: 'typcase match failure!' (ledger row 964). Give each binder a type.
- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. Two calls die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);
  - a read of an exported object's value parameter, from a component that imports the api, where the exporting component names the parameter otherwise than the api. A value parameter is a parameter of the object's constructor, and also a field. An example is `Np(3).a`, where the api declares `object Np(a: ZZ32)` and the component `object Np(z: ZZ32)`. The export check compares no value parameter's name. Give each value parameter the api's name (ledger row 839).

## The checker's gaps

- Overloads: in its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786).
- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the compiled code does not check it. A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
- Imports: `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`. The overloading check also reads `A`'s declarations of a name that the component imports by name from another api. So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`.
- An `except` clause leaves out each identifier that it lists, on both paths. Neither path leaves out an infix operator that it lists. So where a component lists `-` in `except` and declares its own `-` at the api's parameter types, the code generator stops. Walk runs the component's own `-` (ledger row 814).
- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Where a generic type that the clause lists, as `List[\E\]`, gives the body of a member of the trait, the code generator crashes: 'E is not in the kind env' (ledger row 812). Where the variable is a size, a compiled call that passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 307). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).

## The `fortress` commands

`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.

- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.

## Running

    cd ProjectFortress
    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    ../bin/fortress run P [args]

A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.

- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead.

## Before an edit

Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. A status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.

- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'

- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the runtime and B.12 the natives.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'

- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.

## Testing an edit here

- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:

      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java
      rm -rf $Q/caches && cp -a default_repository/caches $Q/caches
      java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "$Q/classes:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile P.fss
      bin/fortress run P

  For a Scala file, compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d $Q/classes -encoding UTF-8 X.scala`. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).

## The checker's time

This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.

The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 to 180 seconds, more under load. It can run past the Bash tool's 120-second limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.

The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):

1. The type hierarchy and the type check.
2. The overloading check, which also compares the overloads' return types.
3. In the component only, the export check (`library.md`, "Designing a change").

So the count misses the errors of the later stages, and a fix of an early error can raise it.

The table's rows tell a clean run from a run that the checker did not finish:

- `#total 0` and `#locations 0`: the checker reached the component and found no error.
- `#stopped`, in place of `#total` and `#locations`: the errors came from a phase before the checker, such as the parse. The checker reported none and did not reach the component. The script exits 1, and the gate reads the table as red.
- `#crash`: the first crash of the overloading check that the run survived, or `none`.

If the run printed no error total and was not clean, the script writes no table and exits 1.

The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:

- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.

A node's hash starts from its class name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks, does not vary from run to run. A moved order is a difference: keep the old order, or report it.

`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.

   inside `atomic do ... end` by the two implicit threads of a
   `do ... also do ... end`.

   Specification/basic/expressions/atomic.tex, section "Atomic Expressions" requires the read and the
   write of `counter` to appear to occur in a single atomic step with respect
   to any action of a thread dynamically outside, so the two threads together
   must perform exactly 2 * iterations increments.  atomic.tex, section "Atomic Expressions" gives the
   same shape as the chapter's own example: a loop body that reads and writes a
   shared counter inside `atomic`, which "will appear to occur atomically with
   respect to all other threads -- including both other iterations of the loop
   body".

   The increment is in a top-level function rather than written out in the loop
   body so that this program tests transaction membership alone; assignment
   from inside a nested code-generation context is the other half of the same
   repair and MutableTopLevelVarInLoop.fss covers it.

   the count is read once from the environment (FORTRESS_THREADS,
   runtimeSystem/FortressExecutable.java:37-44) and Java cannot set an
   environment variable for its own process.  Nor does the gate set one: the
   fastTrack macro that runs compiler_tests sets FORTRESS_CACHES and no thread
   count (build.xml:927-953), and the harness runs each program in a

   not the implementation is correct.  The deterministic half of the repair,

   carries the gate.  Runs both ways are in

content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

An assignment expression consists of a left-hand side
(\emph{AssignLefts}) indicating one or more variables, subscripted
expressions (as described in \secref{subscripted-assignment}), or
field accesses to be updated, an assignment token, and a
right-hand-side expression.  Multiple left-hand sides must be grouped
using tuple notation (comma-separated and parenthesized).  Variables
updated in an assignment expression must already be declared.

The assignment token `\EXP{\ASSIGN}' indicates ordinary assignment.
Ordinary assignment proceeds in two phases.  In the first, the evaluation phase, the
right-hand-side expression is evaluated in parallel with each of the
left-hand-side subexpressions, forming an implicit thread group.
Evaluating a left-hand variable does nothing.  Evaluating a left-hand
field reference evaluates the receiving object.  Evaluating a
left-hand subscripting operation evaluates the receiving object and
the index in parallel in a nested thread group.  After the outer
implicit thread group completes normally, the assignment phase begins.  Each component of the right-hand-side value is
assigned to the corresponding component of the left-hand side in
parallel, forming an implicit thread group.  Assigning a left-hand
variable simply changes the binding for the variable's location to

<!-- Rung D of climb batch 32, the record lines for the gather: the FACTS entry, the rows closed, the new rows, the handover line and the revival change. -->

# Rung D, rung-tuple-binding: record lines

## Finding

A top-level binding of several names to one right side compiles and runs on the compiled path, at commit `47aad62914`. The checker types each name by its element, or by its declared type: a numeral element takes its default at an untyped name (`ZZ32`, `RR64`), and its declared type's conversion at a typed one. The code generator evaluates the right side once, into a hidden top-level variable `<Component>$tuple$<first name>`, at the first read of any of the names, and makes each name a top-level variable of its own class, immutable or mutable, exported and imported as any other. A wildcard binds nothing. It holds for a right side that is a tuple expression, a call or a variable of tuple type, for the forms `(a, b) = e`, `(a: T, b: U) = e`, `(a, b): (T, U) = e`, `(a, b): T... = e`, `var (a, b): (T, U) = e` and `(a, b): (T, U) := e`. Evidence: `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/TopLevelTupleBindingCompiled.test`, `TopLevelTupleBindingImport.test` and `XXXTopLevelTupleBindingType.test`, 'OK (7 tests)' with `XXXTopLevelVarByAssignExport.test`; `ant testQuick` `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` (86, 263 and 1576 tests, 0 failures); the atomic runs 66 of 66 `PASS`; the count stage `#total 0`, `#crash none`, equal to climb batch 30's table; the distance stage `DISTANCE SAME 0`; three files of the baseline ladder UP from `codegen` to `pass` (`tests/TupleBinding.fss`, `tests/TupleBinding2.fss`, `tests/Variable.VarWTypes.fss`). What it means for the work: the model's lines 17 to 19 need no other form on the compiled path; under the distance stage's driver they are three `@@CG OK`, and `MicroGptFlat.fss` goes from 8 distinct checker sites to 9 against the one library: `:41` is gone, which was this defect, and `:77`, `beta1 m`, an `RR64` times an unsized array, is new twice, which row 474 hid. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-tuple-binding/REPORT.md`.

## For FACTS

**A top-level tuple binding compiles: each name is a top-level variable of its element's type, and the right side is evaluated once, at the first read of any name.** The checker gives the tuple that it rebuilds from the checked elements their tuple type, from which each name's thunk reads its own (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Decls.scala:272-277`); the code generator keeps the right side's value in a hidden class `<Component>$tuple$<first name>` and gives each name its own class, whose initializer takes its element out by the tuple's typed getter (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:6528`). So a model line of this form compiles as written, and a name bound so is typed as a single binding's is. Under walk the same right side runs once for each name and once more (row NEW-D-1). Test: `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/TopLevelTupleBindingCompiled.test`. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-tuple-binding/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "The binding as compiled".

## Rows closed

- Row 988: `ledger.py close 988 --commit 47aad62914 --test TopLevelTupleBindingCompiled`.
- Row 474: `ledger.py close 474 --commit 47aad62914 --test XXXTopLevelTupleBindingType.test`. The row's two refusals are `z: String = headDim`, which the test pins, and `zz0: ZZ32 = beta1`, 'Right-hand side has type RR64, but declared type is ZZ32.', which REPORT.md's table holds.

## Changes to other rows

- Row 152, a note: `under walk the right side of such a binding runs once for each name and once more (row NEW-D-1)`. Checked with `ledger.py note 152 TEXT --check` at a three-digit number: it fits, and leaves the notes about 8 characters of 700. The row's notes also say of an earlier model program's `(corpusTokens, corpusLengths) = loadCorpus(corpusPath)` that "the corpus loads once, on import as on run"; by row NEW-D-1 that right side runs three times under walk. I did not run that program, which is only in git history, so the row's words are left to the record pass.

## New rows

Section "3. Traits, objects and components". Linted with `ledger.py check --rows`: each fails only the number rule.

| NEW-D-1 | under walk the right side of a top-level tuple binding is evaluated once for each name and once more: `(first, second) = pairOnce()` runs `pairOnce` three times, and the names hold elements of different runs | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (walk) | `basic/variables.tex`, "Top-Level Variable Declarations" | ProjectFortress/tests/XXXTopLevelTupleBindingOnceWalk.fss | climb batch 32 rung D | siblings: 152. `DesugarerVisitor.forVarDecl` binds a temporary to the right side, then initializes each name from a field reference on the right side itself, not on the temporary (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/rewrite/DesugarerVisitor.java:865-875`, at db352c1776). With a counter in `pairOnce`, `calls` is 3, `first` 2 and `second` 30; three names give four runs. A tuple of literals shows only its cost. The compiled path evaluates once (`compiler_tests/TopLevelTupleBindingCompiled`). Workaround: bind the call to one name, `pair = pairOnce()`, then `(first, second) = pair`. |
| NEW-D-2 | under walk a top-level initializer whose call reads a mutable top-level variable declared later fails: `early = next()` before `var counter: ZZ32 = 5`, with `next(): ZZ32 = counter + 1`, 'Failed to find any matching overload, args = (thunk …' | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (walk) | `basic/variables.tex`, "Top-Level Variable Declarations" | ProjectFortress/tests/XXXInitializerCallReadsLaterMutableWalk.fss | climb batch 32 rung D | siblings: 323. The specification lets an initializer refer to a variable declared later. Walk runs an initializer that reads a later mutable variable itself (`ProjectFortress/tests/InitOrderWithMutable.fss`); read in the body of a function that the initializer calls, the variable's unevaluated thunk reaches the operator. With the later variable immutable walk prints 6, as the compiled path does in both forms. At db352c1776. Workaround: declare the mutable variable before the initializer that reaches it. |
| NEW-D-3 | the compiled export check does not match a top-level variable that a component declares mutable by `:=` against the api's `var` declaration: `tally: ZZ32 := 0` under `var tally: ZZ32`, 'Unmatched declarations … due to different modifiers' | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (checker) | `basic/variables.tex`, "Top-Level Variable Declarations" | ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXTopLevelVarByAssignExport.test | climb batch 32 rung D | siblings: 844. The specification: the modifier `var` is optional when `:=` is used. The export check compares the declarations' modifiers, and `:=` sets the variable mutable without the modifier. The same for a tuple binding, `(a, b): (ZZ32, ZZ32) := (0, 9)`. Walk runs a program that imports such a variable. At db352c1776. Workaround: write `var` in the component. |

## Handover line

Rung D landed on `wip/rung-tuple-binding` at `47aad62914`: a top-level tuple binding compiles, rows 988 and 474 close, the model's lines 17 to 19 pass the code generator, and `MicroGptFlat.fss:77` (`beta1 m`, an `RR64` times an unsized array) is a checker site that row 474 hid; three defects met on the way have `XXX` tests and rows NEW-D-1 to NEW-D-3, of which NEW-D-1 (walk runs such a right side once for each name and once more) is a one-word repair in `DesugarerVisitor.java:873` that waits for the curator.

## Revival change

**The change.** The team's code generator refuses a top-level declaration of several names: `forVarDeclPrePass` throws 'VarDecl … tupled lhs not handled.' where the left side has more than one name (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:6475-6477` at `db352c1776`), and the team's checker, in its case for a tuple expression of as many elements, rebuilds the right side without a type, so that each name has none (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Decls.scala:270-272` at `db352c1776`). The tree now compiles the form: each name is a top-level variable of its declared type or its element's type, a numeral element at its default, and the right side is evaluated once, when the first of its names is read (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/TopLevelTupleBindingCompiled.test`). A use of a name at another type is refused (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXTopLevelTupleBindingType.test`, whose prefix is the harness's mark of a compile that must fail). The reason: the specification gives the form for every top-level declaration, "All forms can be used with tuple notation to declare multiple variables together" (`Specification/basic/variables.tex:99`), and a variable's value "is computed to be the value of the initializer expression" (`:63`); walk's own desugaring states the same design, "Introduce a temporary, then initialize elements piece-by-piece" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/rewrite/DesugarerVisitor.java:858-859`). Walk departs from it: its right side runs once for each name and once more (`ProjectFortress/tests/XXXTopLevelTupleBindingOnceWalk.fss`).

**Provenance.** The item: rows 988 and 474 of the gap ledger, and the model's hyperparameter lines, which P-9 keeps as tuple bindings. The default it follows: fork D1 of CLIMB-BATCH-32.md, "Each name of a tuple binding is a top-level variable of its element's type; the right side is evaluated once", and fork D2, the code generator's half for a top-level binding only; P-173 for a numeral element's default. The batch: climb batch 32, rung D.

\section{Coercions for Tuple and Arrow Types}
\seclabel{coercion-tuple-arrow}

Unlike other types, tuple types (described in \secref{tuple-types}) and
arrow types (described in \secref{arrow-types}) are
not defined explicitly.  Therefore coercions to these types are also
not defined explicitly.  Instead, the following rules describe when
these coercions are implicitly defined.

There is a coercion from a tuple type $\VAR{X}$ to a tuple type
$\VAR{Y}$ if all the following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$\VAR{X}$ is not a subtype of $\VAR{Y}$;

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

### 1. A defect of the change: a declared name beside names without a type was not checked (`a29032ee89`)

Finding. Where only some names of a top-level tuple binding declare a type, and the right side is no tuple expression of as many elements, the checker's general case typed the names without one from the right side and kept the declared ones as written, unchecked (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Decls.scala:318-323`). The base's code generator stopped every such program; the rung's code generator compiles it, so the program ran ill-typed: a loud stop became a quiet value or a failure of the JVM's verification.

Settled by: "The static type of expr must be a subtype of Type" (`Specification/basic/variables.tex:65`), "All forms can be used with tuple notation" (`:99`), and "There is a coercion from a tuple type X to a tuple type Y if …" (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:768`), which the checker already applies where every name declares a type.

The ways: (a) signal where an element's type is no subtype of the declared type, which would refuse `(total: ZZ64, part) = two()` though the fully typed form and walk convert it; (b) check the right side again against the tuple of each name's type, declared or read from the first check. Taken: (b), in the top-level case only, 12 lines (`Decls.scala:324-336`). A single binding does not reach it: one name declares a type or none does. The local case has the same gap and is left as it is, since a local tuple binding's typing is a reserved point and the interpreter's library, which the count stage checks, has local tuple bindings: row NEW-D-4.

    [junit] Tests run: 86, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
    [junit] Tests run: 263, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
    [junit] Tests run: 1585, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
    BUILD SUCCESSFUL

The run held `XXXTupleBindingFloatElementCompiled`, a first form of NEW-D-5's test whose essence was wrong; `XXXBlockEndsInTupleOfNumeralCompiled` replaced it afterwards, two cases for two, and is in the `OK (16 tests)` run. No count or distance stage ran after the fixes: the report's tables are those of the worker's head, and the gate's tables on the merged tree are the record. The atomic runs were not repeated: the fixes change no code of a mutable variable's class.

## Where I differ from the worker's account

- The record's finding said that the form holds for names typed one by one over a call. It did not where other names had no type; it does after fix 1.
- Decision 3 of the report, a binding of wildcards only emits nothing: the right side is then never evaluated on the compiled path (`(_, _) = (note(), note())` above). It follows the lazy single variable and is part of the worker's second question for the curator; I add it there.
- The report's "before" for the model's lines is the planner's run, not a run of the worker's on the base; the planner's note holds it (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/model-closure-check.md:45-58`), and my own program of the three lines stops on the old code as that note says.

## The failure-mode question

The rung turned a stop of the compile into a running program. Where the value is quiet: a wildcard-only binding's right side never runs, and a binding's right side runs at the first read of a name, not at load (the worker's second question). The mixed binding's unchecked name was the one quiet wrong value, repaired by fix 1. A cyclic binding with declared types ends in a Java exception on both paths, as a single cyclic variable does.

## Verdict

Approved. The change does what the section asks, test first; with fix 1 a declared name of a top-level tuple binding is checked in every form. Rows 988 and 474 close as `record.md` says; rows NEW-D-1 to NEW-D-6 are new.

### 1. A defect of the change: a declared name beside names without a type was not checked (`a29032ee89`)

Finding. Where only some names of a top-level tuple binding declare a type, and the right side is no tuple expression of as many elements, the checker's general case typed the names without one from the right side and kept the declared ones as written, unchecked (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Decls.scala:318-323`). The base's code generator stopped every such program; the rung's code generator compiles it, so the program ran ill-typed: a loud stop became a quiet value or a failure of the JVM's verification.

Settled by: "The static type of expr must be a subtype of Type" (`Specification/basic/variables.tex:65`), "All forms can be used with tuple notation" (`:99`), and "There is a coercion from a tuple type X to a tuple type Y if …" (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:768`), which the checker already applies where every name declares a type.

The ways: (a) signal where an element's type is no subtype of the declared type, which would refuse `(total: ZZ64, part) = two()` though the fully typed form and walk convert it; (b) check the right side again against the tuple of each name's type, declared or read from the first check. Taken: (b), in the top-level case only, 12 lines (`Decls.scala:324-336`). A single binding does not reach it: one name declares a type or none does. The local case has the same gap and is left as it is, since a local tuple binding's typing is a reserved point and the interpreter's library, which the count stage checks, has local tuple bindings: row NEW-D-4.

The atomic runs were not repeated: the fixes change no code of a mutable variable's class.

## Where I differ from the worker's account

- The record's finding said that the form holds for names typed one by one over a call. It did not where other names had no type; it does after fix 1.
- Decision 3 of the report, a binding of wildcards only emits nothing: the right side is then never evaluated on the compiled path (`(_, _) = (note(), note())` above). It follows the lazy single variable and is part of the worker's second question for the curator; I add it there.

The rung turned a stop of the compile into a running program. Where the value is quiet: a wildcard-only binding's right side never runs, and a binding's right side runs at the first read of a name, not at load (the worker's second question).
